{{DISPLAYTITLE:Lean and physics}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A proof checker can do one thing for physics: check that a conclusion follows from
stated assumptions. It cannot check that the assumptions describe the world. This page says what that
division means in practice, how real numbers, units and approximations enter a formal statement,
and what has been done in Lean on physics so far. It closes with this wiki's own physics.

== A derivation, as Lean sees it ==

A derivation in physics starts from laws and assumptions and arrives at a result. In Lean the
laws and assumptions become hypotheses, the result becomes the statement, and the derivation
becomes the proof. Here a body is assumed to move at a constant speed <code>v</code>, and the
theorem says how far it moves between two times:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem displacement (x : Int → Int) (x₀ v : Int)
    (law : ∀ t, x t = x₀ + v * t) (t₁ t₂ : Int) :
    x t₂ - x t₁ = v * (t₂ - t₁) := by
  rw [law t₂, law t₁]
  grind
</pre>

Lean accepts it. What it has checked is a conditional: if the position <code>x</code> follows
the law named <code>law</code>, then the displacement is speed times elapsed time. It has not
checked that any body moves that way. Whether one does is a question for measurement, and no
proof can answer it. (The example uses whole numbers so that it runs in Lean without any library;
the same statement over the real numbers needs Mathlib.)

The project this wiki records puts the point in one line: Lean proves the model, not the world
(see [[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the move to Lean]]).

== What Lean can and cannot check ==

Lean can check that every step of a derivation is valid, that no case is skipped, and that the
assumptions used are exactly the ones stated. An assumption that a written derivation uses without
saying so becomes, in Lean, a hypothesis that must be written down, or else the proof fails.

Lean cannot check three things. It cannot check that the assumptions are true of nature; that is
what experiments are for. It cannot check that the symbols stand for the things they are meant to,
that <code>x</code> really is a position measured from a chosen point; that link between the
mathematics and the world is made by people. And it cannot check that the statement proved is the
one that was wanted (see [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Stating the right thing|stating the right thing]]).

== Real numbers ==

Physics is written over the real numbers, and core Lean has none (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/A library of mathematics|a library of mathematics]]). Mathlib
defines them as classes of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers, sequences whose terms get and
stay arbitrarily close to one another.<ref name="real">Mathlib, source file <code>Mathlib/Basic/Real/Basic.lean</code>, module documentation "Real numbers from Cauchy sequences". [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Basic/Real/Basic.lean github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
These are the exact real numbers of mathematics, not the rounded numbers a computer calculates
with. A theorem about real numbers therefore says nothing by itself about the rounding errors of a
numerical simulation. Connecting the two takes a further statement, one that bounds the error.

== Units ==

On paper, units are checked by hand. In Lean they can be made part of the types, so that adding a
length to a time is refused before any proof begins. A small version:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
structure Metres where
  val : Int

structure Seconds where
  val : Int

instance : Add Metres := ⟨fun a b => ⟨a.val + b.val⟩⟩

def d : Metres := ⟨3⟩
def t : Seconds := ⟨2⟩

#eval (d + d).val
</pre>

Lean prints <code>6</code>: two lengths add. A length and a time do not:

<pre class="lean lean-cont lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#eval (d + t).val
</pre>

Lean answers: failed to synthesize instance of type class, naming the missing addition of
<code>Metres</code> and <code>Seconds</code>. A fuller treatment exists. A 2025 preprint formalised
dimensional analysis in Lean: a dimension is a map from base dimensions to their exponents, dimensions
form a group under multiplication, physical quantities pair a value with a dimension, and the
framework covers SI units, fundamental constants and the Buckingham Pi theorem, with the
Lennard-Jones potential as a worked case.<ref name="dims">Maxwell P. Bobbin, Colin Jones, John Velkey and Tyler R. Josephson, "Formalizing dimensional analysis using the Lean theorem prover", arXiv:2509.13142, 16 September 2025. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13142 arxiv.org/abs/2509.13142]</ref>

== Approximations ==

Physics leans on approximations: small angles, weak fields, slow speeds. The sign "≈" means
nothing to Lean. An approximation has to be stated as an exact claim, usually an inequality with an
explicit bound on the error, or a statement about a limit. Writing it out that way shows what the
approximation actually assumes: how small the angle must be, and how large the error can then get.
That can be harder than the derivation it serves, and it is part of what formal proof adds.

== Physics in Lean so far ==

In 2024 Joseph Tooby-Smith introduced '''HepLean''', a project to formalise high energy physics in
Lean 4, with first examples from flavour physics (CKM matrices), local anomaly cancellation and
Higgs physics. Its stated aims include making results easier to find, helping new results to be
found by artificial intelligence and automated methods, making the mathematical checking of papers easier, and new ways of
teaching.<ref name="heplean">Joseph Tooby-Smith, "HepLean: Digitalising high energy physics", ''Computer Physics Communications'' 308 (2025), article 109457. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpc.2024.109457 doi:10.1016/j.cpc.2024.109457]; preprint arXiv:2405.08863.</ref>
HepLean was renamed PhysLean and later merged with Lean-QuantumInfo, a library for quantum
information, to form '''Physlib''', an open-source community project under the Apache 2.0 licence
that depends on Mathlib. Its core library holds reviewed formalisations; a separate area with
lighter review accepts larger and faster contributions, including some generated by AI.<ref name="physlib">''Physlib'' (README). [https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib github.com/leanprover-community/physlib], consulted 14 October 2026; also [https://physlib.io physlib.io].</ref>

Formalisation has also found a mistake. In 2026 Tooby-Smith formalised a widely cited paper of 2006,
by Maniatis, von Manteuffel, Nachtmann and Nagel, on the stability of the two-Higgs-doublet
potential, and found an error in its arguments that invalidates its main theorem on stability. He
suggests that this may be the first non-trivial error in a physics paper found through
formalisation.<ref name="2hdm">Joseph Tooby-Smith, "Formalizing the stability of the two Higgs doublet model potential into Lean: identifying an error in the literature", arXiv:2603.08139, version 2, 20 April 2026. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08139 arxiv.org/abs/2603.08139]</ref>
[[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Physics in Lean|Physics in Lean]] describes this work further.

== This wiki's physics ==

The physics editions on this wiki, [[Hamilton's principle]], [[Noether's theorems]] and
[[On Physical Lines of Force]], are written in ordinary mathematics and prose, not in Lean.
The framework this wiki records is moving to Lean (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Principia Machina|Principia Machina]]). Its own account notes
that physics over the real numbers needs Mathlib, which it has not yet chosen to adopt
(see [[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the move to Lean]]).
